title: A missing teenager was found after she reached out to another Among Us player for help
author: Vikki Blake
content:
"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim."

A teenager who went missing in Utah more than 17 months ago has been rescued from a home in Oregon after she got in touch with another young player in Among Us.

According to a federal criminal complaint reported by Newsweek and KUTV (via IGN), the girl, who was 15 when she disappeared from Garden City, Utah, on 29th May 2025, began chatting with another teenager in Among Us on or around 15th October this year.

The pair later moved their conversation to a different social media app, where she told them who she was and that she was being held against her will in Oregon. She had been given a phone with no cellular data, which meant she could only get online via wi-fi.

The other teen told their parent, who contacted the FBI on 1st November. Agents listened in on a video call between the parent and the girl, and she was recovered from the house later that day. She is now 17.

Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, of Huntington, Oregon, was arrested during a traffic stop.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Utah, he allegedly met the girl online in May 2025, then drove to Utah to pick her up and took her back to his home across state lines. He was charged on 2nd November with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity, and made his first court appearance in Boise, Idaho, on 4th November.

"Our priority in this case was the safe return of the minor victim," said US Attorney Melissa Holyoak. "Those who allegedly exploit and prey upon the most vulnerable members of our communities will be relentlessly investigated and held accountable."

Utah's US Attorney's Office stresses that a complaint is merely an allegation, and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

title: Warren Spector pops off at EA executives and their massive payouts as BioWare shuts down: "Is there any accountability left in this world?"
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
"Obviously not."

It's only been two weeks since we last heard Warren Spector sound off about EA's sudden decision to close BioWare, following the publisher's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF and venture capitalist concerns. But now, the storied developer is back and - apparently - angrier than ever.

"I recently posted my thoughts about EA’s shuttering of BioWare," Spector wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "Those of you who read my post know that I was unhappy. I remain so. The tragedy of so many layoffs the last few years hasn’t been lost on me, but for some reason, BioWare hit me on an emotional level that nothing before had. I felt gut-punched."

Spector goes on to counter the idea that the studio was closed down as a "sound business decision" because the "studio’s glory days (artistic and commercial) were behind them" and that "businesses don’t succeed on history alone". These reactions, more than anything else, appear to be what's inspired Spector to take to posting again - he simply cannot agree with this assessment.

"If studio-level people leave, resulting in dilution of talent, someone is creating an environment that pushes them out. Do those culture-killers pay any price? If executives misread the market, over-hire, or make decisions that result in under-funded, over-funded, poorly-marketed games do they lose sleep let alone jobs?" he asks.

"Do those same executives suffer like developers when the needs of financial partners and private investors take precedence over the people who actually create value, let alone over the interests of players? Does anyone up there in or adjacent to the C-suite care? Is there any accountability left in this world? Obviously not."

He then goes on to list the yearly payouts that some of the highest-level executives at EA are rewarded per annum. These include:

  • Andrew Wilson (chief executive officer): $38.65 million
  • Laura Miele (president)t: $13.7 million
  • Stuart Canfield (chief financial officer): $11.3 million
  • Jake Schatz (chief legal officer): $8.4 million
  • Mala Singh (chief people officer): $8.3 million

"Tens of thousands of do-ers and makers are out of work and these people think they're worth that kind of compensation?" continues Spector. "And if you think this is a discussion about 'sound business decisions', I hope you never get anywhere near running a business. Or at least that people have the sense not to go work for you."

Back in August, we saw Warren Spector announce his intention to retire from the world of video game development. Spector's announcement comes shortly after the last game he worked on - Thick as Thieves - had its final major update only a few months after its release. Despite its charm and low price, Thick as Thieves sadly didn't sell what it needed to, resulting in layoffs at Spector's studio.

title: Star Wars Zero Company sold over a million copies. Its studio has just laid off staff
author: Vikki Blake
content:
"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together."

Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor has laid off an unspecified number of staff, a month after bringing some of its furloughed team back to work.

Several developers announced on LinkedIn on Friday, 6th November, that they had been let go, as first reported by Bespin Bulletin. Bit Reactor hasn't said how many people are affected.

Among them is senior environment artist Ryan Lopez, who spent three and a half years working on Zero Company, from pre-production to launch, and was laid off after a three-month furlough. UI engineer Tyler Eichten, who worked on much of the on-screen UI for the game's tactical missions, and Ryan Mosher from the QA team have also confirmed they were let go.

"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together," Lopez wrote. "It was a privilege to ship a game with you."

Bit Reactor furloughed most of its staff in the weeks before Zero Company launched on 27th August, with one source putting the figure at roughly 80 percent. The studio appeared to have run out of money just short of release.

The game did well regardless, and is thought to have sold more than a million copies within a month. Then, in a message shared on Bluesky on 7th October, CEO Greg Foertsch said the studio had "started the process of returning more of our team back to work". Asking staff to step away so close to launch was "an incredibly difficult decision", he said, "but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible".

It's thought more than half the studio returned, though not everyone went back on full pay. It's not clear whether any of those who returned were among the people laid off this week.

In Eurogamer's Star Wars Zero Company review, we awarded the game four out of five stars, saying, "an already winning genre is matched with the perfect setting in this earnest, heartfelt, smart and slightly ramshackle turn-based tactics gem".

title: Soulframe to launch into free open alpha this week after spending three years closed to the public, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever
author: Connor Makar
content:
Plenty Pact in too!

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of an alpha) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) review - this Switch 2 remake has reminded me Nintendo's masterpiece is still worth talking about for a reason
author: @eurogamer
content:
Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve.

I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded.

Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule.

So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it.

Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards.

Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2.

Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper.

Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly.

Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play.

My favourite locations of all, however, are two of the mid-game dungeons. The Water Temple is now a drowned Art Nouveau palace that you could easily imagine Captain Nemo knocking around in. And the Forest Temple, which is my absolute favourite Zelda dungeon of all time, is a parquet-floored murder mansion that's been overtaken by trees. Dark wood-panelled corridors and weird bits of church sticking out of the foliage. It's the kind of place you'd hear a weird crime podcast about.

Trade-offs, however. My wife, a huge fan of the original game, would wander in and out as I played, and often felt the game she remembered was a little more characterful in its visuals. The moment you fight Dark Link, for example, has lost a little of its glitchy liminality, although the staging, with an old tree in the middle of a vast smoky room, is still wonderfully strange. Towards the end of the game, with the trip into Gerudo territory, you could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment. It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore.

All that, and some strange character models that inevitably I learned to love, don't really matter very much, however. Not least because a handful of clever tweaks elsewhere mean that Ocarina now races along at an astonishing clip. And all this with a careful paring back of intrusions from Navi the fairy and the owl, who were both there in the original game to help move you along swiftly in the first place.

These tweaks are all pretty great. Link now has a jump button, which removes the original game's contextual jumps from the equation, and makes the thundering jump attack even more pleasing to pull off. Even better, in a loan from the 3DS remake of Ocarina, you can swap out usable items using a trigger mini-menu, and you can change boots and whatever you had on your head with some of the directional face buttons.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

This doesn't sound like much, but it's quietly transformative in the way that the best updates are. Take the Water Temple. This is the stuff of memes in terms of difficulty and the patience required in navigating an environment that can be flooded up to three different levels. But now, as on the 3DS, you can enjoy it without having to slip into the menu every few steps to add your iron boots or remove them.

And this in turn means that a dungeon I had been really dreading turned out to be a dungeon that revealed itself via experimentation. I would change the water level and see what options I now had, think about the relationship between spaces I could reach and spaces I could not, all without needing to muddle about in menus and interrupt the flow of things. Flow is the word in fact: a simple UI and item-management tweak has given a legendary Zelda dungeon its perfect pace and sense of revelation.

Alongside tweaks like that which I noticed - oh, it's easier to equip the Hookshot - are no doubt hundreds of little things I didn't notice. I suspect there's a lot more gentle direction prompting built into places like the Water Temple, while elsewhere, in the Forest Temple, for example, I suspected that some of the backtracking had been removed. Individual item placements have been changed around perhaps, and there are generous tweaks like a wallet that holds more rupees from the off. For me at least, all of these tweaks had several things in common: they improved the game without removing or altering anything that was particularly meaningful about the original, and, also, I struggled to confidently spot them.

I did try to spot them for a while. And I measured up what I was playing against my memory, which is always wonky in the first place. Hyrule Field feels smaller now, but it's still thrilling to race across. I remember Epona entering the game sooner, or maybe I just remember the idea of a horse in a Zelda game being a huge, attention-holding deal. I thought a favourite boss involving oil paintings came much later, but again, I had just shifted it to the third act because of its original impact on me.

But this gives way over time to the most important thing about Ocarina of Time, I think, and the reason why this remake has such an emotional impact on people like me. This isn't just another Zelda with an ingenious overworld. It's a Zelda game that's even more preoccupied with time than ever before. And this is because time unfolds within the game, via a central mechanic that takes Hyrule seven years into the future, transforming Link from a child to an adult - and then allows you to go back again.

To play a game like this, a game that is about this stuff, after a period of almost thirty years away, gives your imagination and memory a kind of IMAX treatment. I realised that not only is this a game about the passage of time and the way that the world looks different when you're young to when you're a bit older - I had never really realised that adult Link goes through variations of the same dungeons that young Link went through, but now they're all just a bit harder and more consequential - it's also the kind of game that a lot of players have knowingly or unknowingly measured parts of their lives by.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

This time, when I reached the first Fairy Fountain, for example, I remembered that my wife had walked down the aisle to this music - about half the registry office recognised the tune with a shiver of laughter, incidentally. Then there's the Water Temple, which has become cultural shorthand for a challenge that is really not screwing around. How many awful things had I faced in life by first conjuring the spirit of Link about to enter this place.

There's that first arrival in Hyrule Field, which is both a promise of everything that games were about to become in 1998 and that fleeting moment in childhood where the boundaries suddenly change. This game doesn't just send me back into my memories, then. It puts me back in conversation with all the people I have known who have ever loved it. I play it now and think I'm talking to my friend who played it at university, or my wife who loved it long before we met.

Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent? Were the bosses always driven by interesting ideas and drama and humour rather than difficulty? Was the world always so rich with minor characters who linger in the mind - the accordion player in the windmill, the gravedigger who has his own tour he'd really like you to try out? It's impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday. If you're new to Zelda and you're coming to this game fresh, you're going to love it. Someone, somewhere, is about to play a game so special for the first time that they need to call up their friend and tell them all about it. But if you're returning to this game? Well, somehow you'll find that you're still coming to it fresh.

My dad always said that you should read Don Quixote three times in your life, and I only recently realised that he meant that the book changes because you change. So. When I got to the Deku Tree back at the start of Ocarina a few weeks ago, and I completed the dungeon and watched the impossible vision of the Deku Tree dying of weariness? I remembered that the first time I'd been here, almost thirty years ago, I couldn't help but identify with Link, freshly gifted a sword and shield, one dungeon down, ready for whatever came next. This time, I think, I was closer to identifying with the Deku Tree.

And here's the important part: this wasn't a depressing thought. It just meant that I had taken the long route to reach this point, and this astonishing game had taken the long route too. And yet we arrived at this point together, and together we were transformed. And that's really why any of this video game stuff matters.

A copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was provided for this review by Nintendo.

title: Skyblivion team says former volunteer is threatening to sue over code dispute
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Writ happens.

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

title: Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?
author: Brian Fitzpatrick
content:
On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted cert in a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. I am surprised it hasn’t received more press coverage because it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.

Perhaps you think the Supreme Court already hammered in that nail in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, but you’d be wrong. In that case, the court found racial preferences at Harvard and the University of North Carolina to be illegal. Nevertheless, many scholars are now urging schools to turn to what I call “race neutral affirmative action.” These are programs that seek to increase the number of some racial groups relative to others not by selecting for race itself, but by selecting for characteristics correlated with race. For example, instead of using race preferences in admissions, a university uses preferences for applicants who live in zip codes that are nearly all black, applicants who grew up on Indian reservations, or applicants for whom English is a second language. These are real-life examples of what some universities have done when they were forbidden from using race. Many affirmative action supporters think these sorts of things are perfectly legal.

But I have long argued that race proxies are just as illegal as using race itself. My arguments became moot points after the Supreme Court allowed universities to use race itself in admissions in the 2003 case of Grutter v. Bollinger. But now that SFFA has taken that off the table, the question I teed up is back in the limelight: is it constitutional to use racial proxies instead?

That’s what Montgomery County allegedly did to pick the students for its magnet middle schools. Its efforts predated SFFA because, even before the Supreme Court told universities not to use race, they had told school districts not to. In a nutshell, the alleged facts are these: Asian children make up only 15% of the school system’s population – it is majority black and Hispanic – but were taking up half the spots in the magnet middle schools. This didn’t go over well with many parents, so the school board sought to even things out. The board tried several plans but ultimately used a lottery among the applicants who scored above the 85th percentile in their neighborhood on standardized tests. Because the pool was based on how well applicants did compared only to others in their own neighborhood, the plan spread magnet school spots across the county – and, because many neighborhoods don’t have much racial diversity, it spread the spots across the races, too. The number of black and Latino students went up and the number of Asian students went down.

According to Supreme Court precedent, this is unconstitutional. We have a long history of attempts to discriminate indirectly when we couldn’t discriminate directly – and we have an equally long history of the Supreme Court telling us it’s illegal. For example, when we couldn’t deny the ability to vote on the basis of race, we tried using literacy tests and grandfather clauses and felon disenfranchisement instead. The court said those things are illegal. When we couldn’t segregate schools, we tried drawing school district boundaries around mostly black neighborhoods and mostly white neighborhoods instead. The court said we can’t do that, either.

The doctrine is this: if your “purpose” is to discriminate on the basis of race and your “effect” is to discriminate on the basis of race, then you are engaged in discrimination on the basis of race – even if you aren’t using a racial classification. It’s something like the old adage: if something walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck.

Most scholars supported these precedents when people were discriminating against blacks. But now not so much. Thus, I expect a bevy of amicus briefs from academics contorting their way through them. But the contortions I have seen thus far are very weak. For example, the leading theory on why these precedents don’t doom Montgomery County is the old distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination: the purpose to help is different than the purpose to hurt. The precedents involved the purpose to hurt blacks, whereas Montgomery County was trying to help blacks (and Latinos); hurting Asians was just a byproduct, not the purpose.

If you thought the Supreme Court had already rejected – over and over again – the distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination, you’d be right. After all, that’s how we got SFFA. As the court explained there, life is often zero-sum: if you help one race by giving them more spots, you necessarily hurt other races by giving them fewer spots. What is “benign” for one is “invidious” for the others. It’s a distinction without a difference.

The scholars say the cases rejecting the benign-invidious distinction don’t count because they involved racial classifications, not racial proxies. But the court in SFFA anticipated this move and cut it off: “[U]niversities may not simply establish through . . . other means the regime we hold unlawful today. … [W]hat cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. … The Constitution deals with substance, not shadows.” Yes, that’s dicta, but isn’t it very, very probative of what the very same justices will think about the very same question next year?

Moreover, the dicta didn’t come from nowhere: in fact, the Supreme Court has already struck down “benign” racial proxies – a bunch of them. When governments engage in racial gerrymandering of voting districts, they don’t use racial classifications: voters are assigned to one district or another based on where they live, not their skin color. Yet, even when these gerrymanders have been designed to help black and Latino voters, the Supreme Court has struck them down all the same, including just this past term in Louisiana v. Callais. Is not Montgomery County engaged in gerrymandering no less than Louisiana? It’s just school districts, not voting districts.

It is true that the court has required discriminators to try “race-neutral alternatives” before they can use race itself. But the court requires race-neutral alternatives only when discriminators otherwise have a compelling interest to justify their discrimination. All this means is that the court prefers racial proxies to racial classifications when forced to choose; it doesn’t mean racial proxies are insulated from constitutional scrutiny.

Still, the court may not need to get into all this because the question presented in the Montgomery County case merely asks what counts as a discriminatory “effect.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Asian students had to show a “disparate impact” – a term borrowed from Title VII law that means the challenged practice impacts one race more than another – and they couldn’t do so because, even after the gerrymandering, they still comprised a greater portion of the magnet school spots than they did of magnet school applicants.

Although it is true that disparate impact is one way to show a racial effect under the Supreme Court’s purpose-and-effect precedents, as I previously explained, it is not the only way. For example, when the Supreme Court said that school districts couldn’t evade its desegregation decrees by drawing district lines around mostly white neighborhoods and mostly black neighborhoods, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., schools of different quality); it was enough that one school was overwhelmingly white and the other was overwhelmingly black. When the Supreme Court has said that legislatures couldn’t gerrymander voting districts, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., differential vote dilution); it was enough that the racial composition of the districts had been affected.

It is true that what exactly the racial effect is in the voting cases is undertheorized. There is no obvious baseline to compare to the gerrymandered district lines in order to measure the “effect.” For this reason, some scholars think the court has all but read out the effect requirement from the purpose-and-effect test. Maybe so. The effect requirement comes from an old case called Palmer v. Thompson: there, Jackson, Mississippi, closed all their public swimming pools rather than desegregate them; the court held that this wasn’t unconstitutional racial discrimination because all the races had been affected equally. The ruling is unpopular among scholars on the left; law professor Randall Kennedy at Harvard has compared it to Korematsu. Thus, I doubt many will mourn its demise; plaintiffs would still have to show an injury to establish standing in federal court. But overruling it will only help the plaintiffs in the Montgomery County case.

Still, a lingering question that hasn’t been asked enough is whether the purpose-and-effect doctrine – or even a purpose-only doctrine if Palmer goes away – is consistent with the original understanding of the Constitution. It is hard for me to see how it couldn’t be: it is very easy to evade any rule by proxy; surely, they knew that even back in 1868. But I haven’t seen any historical analyses yet. I hope there are some in the briefing.

I appreciate that for many scholars it is inconceivable that we could end up in a world where it is illegal to do anything about racial disparities. Many of them endorse so-called “antiracism” and believe that all racial disparities must be the product of racism – and, indeed, that we, too, are racists if we don’t do something about them. This means we can sometimes have “too many” Asians. Maybe they’re right about that, maybe they’re wrong. But the 14th Amendment does not enact Mr. Ibram X. Kendi’s “How to Be an Antiracist.”

Recommended Citation: Brian Fitzpatrick, Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 2, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/is-montgomery-affirmative-actions-final-chapter/

title: SNL has a new impression of Elon Musk, ‘the worst thing South Africa has ever done’
author: Anthony Ha
content:
Saturday Night Live cast member Jeremy Culhane unveiled his impression of Elon Musk last night, depicting the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as an awkward loser who fumbles his attempt to befriend the hosts of Weekend Update.

This isn’t the first time the show has lampooned the world’s richest man (and one-time SNL host), with Mike Myers dropping by occasionally to wield a chainsaw before freezing and muttering, “Glitch!” 

Since Musk was in the news this week for spending half a billion dollars on candidates who lost in the midterms, then announcing plans to halt Cybertruck production, it’s maybe not surprising that Culhane’s version is a little less obnoxious and a little more desperate to be liked, doing his best to laugh off his setbacks and remind the audience, “My car did a flip!”

Eventually, Weekend Update co-host Colin Jost asks a pointed question about Musk’s week: “You moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats. You moved all your companies to Texas because you didn’t want to pay taxes. You even built your own town in Texas. And now Texas is run by Democrats. Now you’re going to have to pay taxes. So how does that make you feel?”

Culhane nods along with each step of the question, then answers, “Bad?”

To show that he’s a good sport about all this, Culhane also asks his chatbot Grok to do “an epic vulgar roast of me, Elon Musk.” Grok delivers, describing Musk as “the worst thing South Africa has ever done” and suggesting, “Maybe if you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you.”

This week’s episode also featured a spoof of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” featuring Jane Wickline’s uncanny take on the Theranos founder (though most of the jokes focus on episode host Druski).

SNL seems to have its knives out for tech executives this season, starting with Wickline’s impression of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as a stuttering prophet of AI doom.

A couple weeks later, James Austin Johnson caricatured data center backer/”Marty Supreme” co-star Kevin O’Leary. Asked about the widespread public opposition to data centers, Johnson-as-O’Leary smoothly replies, “All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God’s untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job.”

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

title: Russia Haunts Emmanuel Carrère’s New Book
author: @NewYorker
content:
In the fall of 2022, the French writer Emmanuel Carrère visited Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, for the first time. Carrère, who has been called “France’s greatest writer of nonfiction,” was sixty-four at the time; though he was of mixed Russian and Georgian descent—when he visited, his cousin Salomé Zourabichvili, was then serving her fourth year as the country’s President—he had never before set foot in his ancestral homeland.

Why did Carrère wait so long to visit? He asks himself this very question toward the end of his latest book, “Kolkhoz,” a conflicted family history that won the 2025 Prix Médicis. His mother, whose father was the son of a prominent Georgian intellectual and whose own mother was the daughter of a Russian aristocrat, never went at all—she had a fraught relationship with the success of Zourabichvili, whom she treated with “condescending affection.” One would be forgiven for assuming that, as a friend of his joked, Carrère had waited to visit the country until a member of his family was running it. But Carrère’s explanation, characteristically self-effacing, is as shamefully self-interested as it is startlingly frank. “I am my mother’s son, I felt Russian like her, not in the least Georgian,” he writes, “but it’s become so awful to be Russian today that I’m searching for other roots.”

In the course of the past decade or so, there has been a flurry of memoirs and autofictional novels by émigré writers and their descendants, grappling with the challenging inheritance of Russia’s twentieth and twenty-first centuries—the suffering, and the guilt. On the more poised side is Maria Stepanova’s “In Memory of Memory”; on the more beguilingly chaotic is Keith Gessen’s “A Terrible Country.” “Kolkhoz”—along with Evan Gershkovich’s prison memoir, “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” also out this fall—is the most prominent such book to have been published since the beginning of Russia’s war on Ukraine. It is also the most virtuosically, infuriatingly honest.

Carrère, who broke out with his 2000 work of literary true crime “The Adversary,” is one of the most confounding figures in French letters. Written from the surreal intersection of narcissism, self-absolution, and investigative journalism, his books purport to be “about” subjects of general interest—yoga, the iconoclastic Russian writer Eduard Limonov, a perplexing murder spree on the Swiss border—but are, without fail, about himself. More often than not, they are also about his marriages and the extramarital affairs that end them. But, somehow, Carrère never entirely alienates his readers. There’s something refreshing about his frank insistence on his shortcomings, and the way that he manages to neither glorify nor vilify them.

The shortcomings in question are notably pronounced in Carrère’s 2007 memoir, “My Life as a Russian Novel,” which investigates two mysterious disappearances: that of his Georgian maternal grandfather, who vanished after seemingly collaborating with the Nazis in Occupied France, and that of András Toma, a long-lost Hungarian prisoner of war who was discovered in a remote Russian psychiatric hospital at the turn of the millennium. It also brazenly exposes the private life of a Parisian named Sophie, the object of Carrère’s erotic obsession, whose outrage and fascination with him mirrors the reader’s. At one point in the book, Carrère has Sophie declare, “Emmanuel doesn’t vote because he’s afraid he’ll vote for the right.” (Carrère rarely discusses politics, but if he had a conservative bent it would hardly be surprising, given his vocal praise of the works of Michel Houellebecq and Louis-Ferdinand Céline, two of French literature’s biggest provocateurs.)

Carrère can be particularly inflammatory on the subject of Russia. During his research trips to the country in the late nineties and early two-thousands, he befriended, as he put it, “colourful characters who were not necessarily reputable” and devoted years to writing a biography of Limonov, a fervent Russian nationalist opposed to Ukraine’s independence. In other words, no one should look to him for an objective account of Russia’s recent history.

Crucially, an objective account isn’t what he’s produced at all. After all, this is the writer who opened “The Adversary” with the line “On the Saturday morning of January 9, 1993, while Jean-Claude Romand was killing his wife and children, I was with mine in a parent-teacher meeting.” In a Profile for this magazine, Ian Parker described Carrère’s books as enacting “the experience of someone being brought out of himself—diverted from disappointment or dickishness—by the unearthing of a story worth telling and by the desire to be admired for telling it.” For all Carrère’s insensitivity—at one point he refers to sanctions falling on Moscow “like the missiles on Kyiv”—the sense of urgency with which he feels he must tell his family’s story redeems him. It’s not that he thinks doing so will necessarily explain what’s happening in Russia today, or even that it will explain how he feels about the situation, but, rather, that the telling itself is enough.

The birth of “Kolkhoz” coincided with the death of Carrère’s beloved mother, Hélène Carrère d’Encausse, and is concerned almost exclusively with her side of his family. Hélène was born into a world of Russian nobles in exile who transposed their aristocratic geography onto the suburbs of Paris (Meudon, where Hélène grew up, became Miedonsk) and whose Russophone children only began learning French at school. Her Georgian father—from whom she inherited the undeniably foreign surname Zourabichvili, a cause of merciless schoolyard teasing—eventually assimilated completely into his wife’s circle of White Russians. When Hélène married Louis Carrère d’Encausse, a French insurance man, she shed the Georgian designation altogether.

Until adulthood, the only Russia Hélène had ever known was the one these Russians had dreamed up in and around the French capital. Motivated by a desire to preserve this rarefied world, and to learn more about the country that her parents had fled, Hélène enrolled at Sciences Po and became an expert on the region. Later on, she was named the Académie Française’s “perpetual secretary.” In this capacity, she oversaw the latest edition of the French dictionary, and occupied a grand, Académie-provided apartment on the bank of the Seine. By her death at the age of ninety-four, she had become supremely, officially, French. President Emmanuel Macron spoke at her funeral.

It’s ironic that Hélène’s path into the French élite was via her parents’ homeland. Carrère deftly captures his mother’s inner conflict, flipping between contradictory descriptions of her persona: she is at once “proud of her aristocratic and cosmopolitan ancestry” and “French by choice . . . patriotic to the point of chauvinism.” She viewed the rise of Vladimir Putin as a promising development for Russia’s transition toward democracy. Her obstinate sympathy for him not only went against French public opinion; it was also a blow to her cousin Zourabichvili, whose decision to run for Georgia’s President was motivated by Russia’s illegal occupation of the country’s northern territories. The day before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Hélène argued on a TV broadcast that Putin was “a brutal but rational man who looked out for his own interests . . . Of course he would never, ever, do such a crazy thing.”

What prompted Carrère to write “Kolkhoz” was less Russia’s invasion itself than the fact that Hélène was so wrong about it. After Putin’s attack, the French media was as unrestrained in its criticism of Hélène as she had been in her permissiveness toward him. She attempted, soon afterward, to pass her error off as a form of prescience. “If I was wrong, who could have seen clearly?” Carrère relays her saying to others.

In January, 2023, she was profiled by the journalist Raphaëlle Rérolle in Le Monde. The headline read, “The Great Russia Expert ‘Shrouded in Fog.’ ” “Her love of Russia is real, deep-seated,” Carrère writes, paraphrasing the article, “but unfortunately it’s morphed into an indulgence for Putin, so that for twenty years she hasn’t stopped speaking on behalf of the Kremlin at the Élysée, repeating to Chirac, Sarkozy, Hollande, Macron and their successive foreign ministers that Russia is a great country which cannot be judged by our standards, and that Putin is a man of peace.” Hélène was stung by the characterization. Rérolle’s article and the media pile on that followed, Carrère writes, “affected her to such an extent that I heard her say she no longer wanted to live in a world where the supposedly honourable press had reached such depths of ignominy.” His tone crackles with frustration at his mother’s defensiveness. “I’ve reread these articles,” he writes, “they’re harsh, but you can’t really say they’re ignoble, and my mother must have been very unaccustomed to criticism to complain that she was the victim of a media lynching.”

At the time of Hélène’s death, in the summer of 2023, Carrère was grappling with the war in his own, very different way. He was at work on a book about the Black Sea port city of Kherson, and had been travelling back and forth from the front line, collecting accounts of the occupation. “Of all the historical events I’ve witnessed,” he writes, “none has riveted my attention as much as the war in Ukraine.” Around the same time, he became compelled by the fact that, as Russia’s hold on Kherson weakened, in October of 2022, they had exhumed the bones of Prince Grigory Aleksandrovich Potemkin—the Russian Empire’s chief colonizer of the south. The metaphor must have seemed too good to be true: Putin’s Army, despite hemorrhaging men, was preoccupied by preserving the skeleton of the Russian imperial idea. The retreating soldiers took the bones east, into occupied territory, horrified by the thought of them remaining under Ukrainian soil.

What lies beneath the Russian earth—roots, remains, ruined imperial cities—pervades “Kolkhoz,” especially in its portrait of Carrère’s mother. The first time that she visits Soviet Russia as a young woman, during a layover on the way to a research trip in Uzbekistan, Hélène spends her precious few hours riding the Moscow metro, “the deepest and most beautiful in the world, with its mosaics, frescoes, colonnades, chandeliers and mouldings.” Everything touches her: she is even “rocked” by the mundane metro announcement, “Dveri zakryvayutsya. Nie zabyvaete svoi veschi” (“The doors are closing. Do not forget your things”), simply because it is in Russian, the intimate language of her childhood, suddenly writ large. At an underground kiosk, she buys “a map and some postcards,” and naïvely tells the salesclerk behind the counter that she speaks Russian because she’s descended from exiled aristocracy. (The salesclerk, predictably, is less than impressed.)

“She prided herself on understanding the Russians,” Carrère writes, “probing their hearts and souls, vibrating in unison with them”—one imagines a young Hélène literally vibrating in unison with a million strangers in the rattling Soviet cars of the Moscow metro. Despite his pained awareness of his mother’s imperialist delusions, he finds a grain of truth in her conviction that she is in touch with the Russian spirit. If Russia has a collective unconscious, Carrère seems to suggest it might resemble his mother—a proposition in which, against his own better judgment, he clearly finds both pride and comfort.

Like the Russian state, Hélène appears to have buried many disturbing facts as deep down as possible, not least of which is her father’s alleged collaboration with the Nazi regime. It’s chilling to see Hélène’s allegiance to Russian oligarchy prefigured by her youthful affection for the right-wing figures of postwar France. Describing former Nazi collaborators’ visits to the grave of the fascist journalist Robert Brasillach, Carrère sheepishly admits that he’s “far from thrilled to say that my mother, at the age of twenty, consorted with this society of pariahs.”

What emerges from Carrère’s excavation of his mother’s past is a strikingly nuanced portrait of a brilliant, problematic scholar. Moreover, he excels in extrapolating her life onto more than a century of Russian history. In his hands, she becomes a kind of Russian Zelig—a character who appears, conveniently, at every major moment in history throughout her life. She is omnipresent in the immediate aftermath of the Soviet collapse, staying often at the Hotel Ukraina, Moscow’s famous Stalinist skyscraper, and attending events such as “a cocktail party at the French Embassy to celebrate Franco-Soviet scientific exchanges.” Even when she herself is absent, there is always a relative at hand, as in the case of the October Revolution: a great-uncle walks from Petrograd to Finland to escape the Bolsheviks, a family friend is torn to pieces by his serfs.

These historical anecdotes have a scope that brings to mind the great Russian epics. “My Life as a Russian Novel” would have suited the book as a title had Carrère not already used it. In the nineteenth century, Russian literature was instrumental in the formation of the Russkaia dusha, or “Russian soul”—the national myth that Russians are uniquely adept at emotional intensity, spiritual awareness, and suffering. As the twentieth century dispersed Russia’s literati, some left this nostalgic concept behind, while others trailed its shadow with them into exile, burying themselves in the great Russian novels that had formed its foundation. In “Kolkhoz,” it seems to be something of a fixation for Carrère: the émigré dream that Russianness just might be able to exist as a primarily literary mode.

When it comes to this dream, Carrère is caught between competing impulses. On the one hand, Russian literature acts as a means of framing both his reporting and his personal life. On the other, he makes sure to examine it through a post-colonial lens. He and his mother, he notes, are each compelled by the work of Dostoyevsky, entranced by his descent into the darkest, most complex facets of human nature. Hélène’s devotion to the author, “the almost religious conviction that there is nothing better,” is a point of humorous preoccupation throughout “Kolkhoz.” When Carrère discovers a love of Leo Tolstoy’s “War and Peace” in adulthood, he knows his mother will not approve. A friend remarks, sarcastically, “My goodness, what a transgression!”

For Hélène, Dostoyevsky is a symbol of Russian greatness that transcends politics. But, as Carrère acknowledges, in the wake of the Ukraine invasion the author has become an embodiment of Russian nationalism. In the Ukrainian novelist Oksana Zabuzhko’s commanding 2022 essay for the Times Literary Supplement, “Reading Russian Literature after the Bucha massacre,” she convincingly argues that Dostoyevsky was not only a fervent anti-Ukrainian but also a Russian nationalist who constructed an ideology that posed a dangerous question: Can any amount of violence be absolved by surrender to the Russian Orthodox Church? Yes, the ending of “Crime and Punishment” insists: even Rodion Raskolnikov, an infamous perpetrator of senseless violence, can have his Christian awakening in a penal colony in Siberia. “It barely needs pointing out,” Zabuzhko writes, “that Putin’s offensive on February 24 owed much to Dostoevskyism.”

Carrère’s strongest critique of the novelist occurs via proxy. While gathering material in southern Ukraine, Carrère travels with a group of Ukrainian soldiers, one of whom, a brooding young man named Serhiy, reminds him of a character from a Dostoyevsky novel. In an excruciating scene, Carrère, emboldened by more than a few rounds of vodka, decides to begin speaking Russian to his companions, who have made a point of speaking only Ukrainian. None of the soldiers respond, but the next day Carrère’s “Dostoyevskian” figure offers to recount, through a translator, the story of his life. It turns out that Serhiy had been taken prisoner in occupied Donetsk, and subjected to a mock execution. Once he’d finally been freed, he asked his captor why she did what she did. “Because I’m interested in knowing what a man feels when he thinks he’s going to die,” she said. Serhiy replies, without missing a beat, “Read Dostoevsky.” Serhiy, like Zabuzhko, locates his captor’s impulse to torture him in the very pages written by the Russian novelist.

Carrère notes, in passing, that his mother’s “favourite adjective” was “haunted.” “Kolkhoz” is haunted not only by the spectre of his mother but by the question of whether it’s possible to write affectionately, if critically, about Russia today—a question that is at the center of much memoiristic writing about Russia, both by the descendants of those who have left the country, such as Carrère or Evan Gershkovich, and by those who remain.

In the final analysis, perhaps Carrère’s obsession with Russia is not so far removed from his compulsion to write about himself. Writing what he knows, Carrère is consistently, paradoxically insightful on what he doesn’t know. In starting from himself—his childhood, then his mother, then her mother, and so on—he has uncovered something meaningful about the psychology of the Russian Empire that made his grandparents, and those who have followed. More than that, he has masterly evoked an empire just as powerful and just as slippery: the idea of Russia. ♦

title: How an Octopus Can Squeeze into a Beer Can - Nautilus
content:
We’ve long known that octopuses have an uncanny ability to squeeze through small spaces. Whether they prefer beer cans or beer bottles, they’re adept at compressing their bodies to escape danger. But how? A new study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology uncovered some secrets of this octopus refuge behavior.

Lead study author Wenci Xin, a mechanical engineer from the National University of Singapore, and his coauthors from Italy and Austria conducted experiments with three subadult common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) collected by fishermen in France as well as four juvenile Mexican four-eyed octopuses (Octopus maya) raised from eggs in the lab. In multiple trials, each octopus was challenged with passing through a barrier in an acrylic box using either a large hole or a small hole relative to their eye distance. (Octopus eyes sit on either side of their head capsule and thus prove a good proxy for head capsule size.) 

Read more: “How the Rule-Breaking Octopus Is Rewriting the Evolution of Intelligence”

When the hole was relatively large, the common octopuses used a three-step process to get through: 1) explored it with an arm; 2) pushed most of their other arms through; and 3) reached back with an arm to leverage the rest of their body and remaining arms through. By anchoring to the acrylic with their arm suckers, they were able to complete the whole maneuver in just 20 seconds. 

When the hole was relatively small, however, they couldn’t put all their arms in at the same time and adapted to a four-step process. The first two steps were the same, but then, instead of dragging their remaining arms through in a bundle with their body, they first jimmied the arms through, followed by the head capsule.

Interestingly, the Mexican octopuses rejected the small holes altogether, not even bothering to try to squeeze through them, instead sitting (sulking?) in the corner of the box. That said, when a large hole was available, they readily adopted the same three-step strategy to pass through the acrylic barrier. 

Xin and the research team hope to apply the time-honed octopus’ strategies to the design of soft search-and-rescue robots, such that they can make it through tight spaces in disaster zones. In that case, octopuses wouldn’t just be saving their own lives by squeezing away from trouble, they’d be saving countless others as well.
